The analysis reveals that the model's generalization is influenced by its training loss, strong connections to structural model characteristics are established under specific assumptions, and the relationship between training and test errors is quantified. The theoretical framework developed can accommodate a broad range of activation functions, including those that exhibit ultraviolet divergence and finite messages, thereby allowing for analysis of overparameterized networks. The generalization bounds obtained are composed of two components: one that reflects the model's ability to fit an underlying data distribution, and another that depends on the model's parameters and is independent of the training set size. The second component is a key innovation of this research and can be viewed as a regularization effect that emerges from the training process. The model's performance is shown to be optimal in certain scenarios, and the influence of the data distribution on generalization is quantified. The analysis also reveals that the traditional view of overfitting needs to be refined, as the model can generalize well even when its training loss is not close to zero.

A previous semantics of GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and recursion model uses infinite sequences, but this paper introduces a small-step semantics that more accurately models GP 2's implementation.  This new semantics includes a small-step operational semantics and an associated small-step abstract semantics, both of which are shown to be equivalent. A fully complete small-step operational semantics has the property that it defines the same behavior for GP 2 as the denotical semantics for GP 2. time-frequency based instantaneously noisy unitary evolution for quantum data protection. We introduce the concept of hidden Subspace Instantaneous Nonlinear Sabotage (HISINS) - a type of noise that safeguards a part of a quantum state's density matrix. We show that a specific type of HISINS noise, $N_{HISINS}^{(1)}$, can protect a two-dimensional subspace of an n-qubit system, achieving this in a time- and time-frequency- scalable manner. Furthermore, we discuss how an alternative noise type, $N_{HISINS}^{(\frac{d}{2})}$, can be utilized to safeguard a unitary $d$-dimensional subspace of a $d$-qubit system, also achieving protection in a time- and time-frequency- scalable manner. We also present a specific noise implementation known as the Hilbert-Schmidt volume noise, which can be utilized to realize $N_{HISINS}^{(1)}$. We also show that a time and time-frequency based instantaneously noisy unitary evolution can be utilized to safeguard a two-dimensional subspace of a quantum system, thereby safeguarding a two-dimensional subspace of a quantum system even when subjected to multiple instances of the Clonotonic noise.

Synthetic control methods create a hypothetical control group by combining historical control values, allowing for treatment impact assessments. A critical issue in synthetic control approaches is the weighting of past control values, as an optimal weighted control series ideally closely mimics the treated entity's behavior. Existing literature suggests that choosing either the full or empty set of past control values yields superior results in theory, although in practice, entities used in weighting often lack sufficient historical data. This study introduces an SCS algorithm, grounded in lasso regression, which allows for selection of an optimal set of control values for weighting. The proposed algorithm is tested across various scenarios, including hypothetical and real-world data scenarios. The results show the effectiveness of the new approach in outperforming traditional synthetic control methods.

This study presents Graph Similarity Network (GSN), a neural network framework capable of learning and evaluating the similarity between directed and undirected graphs based on node and edge attributes. GSN views the similarity between two graphs as a probabilistic distribution over the entire space of possible graphs, given the observed node and edge attributes. few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. The success of this area largely depends on the effectiveness of prototypes learned from a limited number of support samples. A excellent prototype represents the class with the highest accuracy even on unfamiliar queries, and it can be achieved by reducing inter-class differences and increasing intra-class similarity. Support vectors have been traditionally used to build prototypes, yet they are only representative for the data they contain and often fail to generalize to unseen test data. To address this issue, we build prototypes from a prototype-discriminative space by directly building prototypes from the space that categorizes data effectively, known as the prototype-discriminative space. A novel method for building prototypes from the space has been developed, where prototypes are built from the space that categorizes data effectively, and it can be represented by a few key points. The effectiveness of the method known as the PDS method has been demonstrated on various benchmark datasets and models, and it results in the highest performance achieved so far on these datasets and models.

Both involve selecting items from a set to maximize an objective while adhering to a budget limit and a set of nonnegative item values, as well as elements with zero value that contribute to this sum. The primary distinction between these problems lies in the representation of the set, with items either being explicitly listed or implicitly defined through a set of inclusion-exclusion operations. Despite the numerous exact solution algorithms developed for these problems, none have been proposed for the specific case of being NP-hard parameterized by the budget until a recent study on the Set-Union Knapsack Problem. Our investigation builds upon this foundation, presenting similar algorithms for the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, with a particular focus on the relationship between the maximum coverage and the knapsack problem when items are ordered according to their contribution to the solution. Our analysis shows that both problems become fixed-parameter tractable when considering both the budget and the number of elements as parameters, with the Set-Union Knapsack Problem specifically becoming fixed-parameter tractable when the budget is constant and the number of elements is considered.

HMMs are applied across various fields, like speech recognition, DNA sequencing, and image compression algorithms, often used to infer unobservable states given a sequence of observable outputs, after which they are represented as probabilistic state transition diagrams. A novel algorithm, the A* top-down hidden Markov model recognition algorithm, was developed to recognize HMMs by utilizing a limited and adjusted version of the Levenshtein distance metric combined with dynamic programming techniques. This method can be seen as an optimization problem where the probability of the HMM given a sequence of observable outputs is maximized, with the A* method allowing for a more efficient search by limiting the possible states, unfeasible states, and redundant computations. An additional benefit of the A* method is its ability to improve recognition accuracy as the search space evolves, allowing for faster recognition times as the model complexity decreases. The recognition algorithm was applied to a dataset consisting of 50 spoken digits, with the experimental results showing the A* method's superiority to the top-down hidden Markov model recognition algorithm in terms of recognition accuracy and recognition speed.

We introduce a new concept called FROG, which is an efficient method for preserving the privacy of location-based services by utilizing homomorphic encryption. By applying this method to location trajectories within homomorphic encryption environments, the service provider is prevented from accessing or guessing the actual location values. Our evaluation shows that FROG is capable of accurately reproducing the number of locations within a trajectory as well as the distances between them, while keeping the generated trajectories private. We found that the difference between the estimated and real distances is minimal, with an accuracy rate of less than 5% for trajectories containing more than five locations. Furthermore, the privacy level of FROG is superior to other schemes, with a mutual information rate of less than 0.1% between the encrypted and actual trajectories. We also observed that the computational overhead of FROG is manageable, with a processing speed of approximately 8 seconds per location. We conclude that FROG is an efficient and effective method for preserving the privacy of location-based services while maintaining reasonable computational complexity.

3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presentation of this work introduces the DeepPlace framework, a novel, 3D point cloud-based method combining both local and global features for robust place recognition. The proposed framework utilizes a novel architecture consisting of a transformer block paired with a transformer encoder, enabled by the utilization of local and graph features. Local features, generated from the deep point cloud feature association module, employ the deep point graph network to organize and aggregate the association graph, thereby generating 256-bit local features. Graph features, generated from the deep geometric graph network, utilize the geometric graph network to generate 256-bit graph features from the node and edge information. The integration of local and graph features results in the generation of the global graph representation, and ultimately the output of the global place encoding via the transformer decoder. The evaluation of the DeepPlace framework on two benchmark datasets, NuScenes and Waymo, reveals superior performance when utilizing both local and graph features in conjunction with each other.

Utilizing data from the 1000Brains initiative, we demonstrated the importance of site effects in MRI data. We developed a novel, efficient method called FEASIBLe that allows for the removal of site effects from resting-state functional MRI data without requiring prior knowledge or a training set. Unlike existing methods that often rely on regional or network-level statistics, FEASIBLe can directly estimate and filter out site effects from functional connectivity matrices. Our study involved data from 1,011 healthy individuals scanned across 37 sites, which showed that the proposed method effectively removed site effects while preserving class information. Notably, FEASIBLe improved the classification of psychiatric disorders, particularly schizophrenia, using multiple validation datasets with high accuracy (e.g., 91.3% for a Schizophrenia-Healthy comparison, 87.5% for a Schizophrenia-Alzheimer's comparison, and 87.5% for a Schizophrenia/Bipolar Disorder comparison). The feasibility of the approach was further confirmed by using data from the ADNI database, which showed consistent results. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm, FEASIBLe, is capable of removing site effects across multiple datasets, which is essential for cross-site analyses.

iferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition similar to other FeSCs. Recent research on LiFeAs has revealed that it undergoes a nematic state similar to other FeSCs despite the absence of a magnetic transition at low temperatures. This study employed x-ray linear dichroism microscopy to map the electronic structure of LiFeAs around 18 K at a local level. It was observed that LiFeAs exhibits a noticeable asymmetry in its d$_{xz}$ and d$_{xy}$ orbital occupation, exhibiting "snake-like" orbital ordering, in agreement with previous research. This local asymmetry was found to be similar to that observed in magnetically driven nematic FeSCs like Ba(Fe$_{0.92}$Co$_{0.08}$)$_2$As$_2$, suggesting that the nematic modulation in LiFeAs arises from a long-range spatial modulation of the orbital occupation rather than a magnetic transition. This finding supports the idea that the nematic modulation in LiFeAs is responsible for the unusual superconducting characteristics of this compound.

This analysis proposes a novel method for determining the amplitude of the primary type of such B-Mesogenic decay processes, where a B-meson breaks down into a lightest dark particle and a anti-particle from the dark matter sector. This method relies on an approach that involves the fully charmed final state of the B-meson decay, where it breaks down into a charmed meson accompanied by a lightest dark particle and a anti-particle from the dark matter sector. The findings show that the composite fermions theory consistently yields more negative quasiparticle energies than those obtained from the Laughlin theory across all relevant system sizes for two dimensions with a magnetic field intensity of 10 tesla and higher. The reason for this disparity can be attributed to the composite fermions wave function not adhering to the Laughlin wave function's constraint of no composite fermion spin polarization, resulting in an underestimation of quasiparticle energies in composite fermions theory due to an incomplete wave function normalization. To rectify this, we have modified the Slater determinant constructed from composite fermions orbitals into a fully normalized wave function by incorporating a Jastrow factor derived from the composite fermions wave function. The newly developed unitary wave function yields quasiparticle energies that closely align with those calculated from the Laughlin theory. The work of this research showcases a novel method of constructing an effective wave function for composite fermions theory that rivals the Laughlin theory in terms of quasiparticle energy calculations.

This research explores a simplified representation of such a scenario as a system of variational inequalities in two dimensions. By simplifying the problem, we can reframe it as a nonlinear Stokes equation system, and establish the existence and uniqueness of its solution. we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a crucial role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed estimation procedure utilizes an empirical process with finite second moment properties, whose convergence is determined by a Berry-Esseen type theorem. As a result, the asymptotic normality of the estimator is established, along with the derivation of a quantifiable expression for the rate of convergence. Our study also establishes the validity of the central limit theorem for the square root of the estimated correlation, provided that sufficient data points exist. Furthermore, a robust version of the correlation coefficient has been developed, which emerges as a smooth version of the maximum of suitably normalized Kendall's tau values. The behavior of this new statistic is analyzed using techniques from extremal theory, with the goal of creating a robust correlation coefficient that can withstand outliers while retaining its correlation properties.

This risk could potentially be mitigated by limiting access to such data, although this would come at the known cost of deep RL's slow convergence rates. This study takes a different approach, focusing on restricting data access in a manner that provides conceptual insight into the trade-off between risk and performance. We achieve this by incorporating a regularization term derived from the data access constraint into the actor-critic agent's objective function. As a result, our proposed method, DACTR, significantly improves convergence rates while limiting data access. Furthermore, DACTR's regularization term provides an upper bound on the data access risk, demonstrating its importance. Experiments show that on data-sensitive tasks such as Atari games, DACTR substantially improves convergence and achieves substantially safer performance compared to off-policy agents.

Although existing consensus protocols can handle up to a certain level of failure, creating robust consensus protocols that work even when multiple components fail is extremely challenging. The key challenge here is designing a consensus protocol that allows a majority of the system components to agree on a single value even when multiple components fail. The well-known Chord protocol is used for peer-to-peer file sharing, but it does not support consensus. The Chained Consensus protocol, on the other hand, can be used to support consensus, however, it fails when a certain number of components fail. We propose a new distributed consensus protocol called DvChain, which works with any number of failed components. The DvChain protocol works by breaking down the consensus task into smaller sub-tasks called links, and using these links to represent the consensus value. Each component in the system is then linked to each other, and the value of the consensus is represented by the order in which components are linked to each other. The DvChain protocol works by allowing components to fail, but it ensures that a majority of the system components agree on a single value even when multiple components fail. We compare the methods to a composite score based on syntactic complexity, which takes into account the frequency of multiple syntactic categories for words and the complexity of syntactic patterns. The evaluation considers how accurately each measure reflects the known complexities of languages. We also compare the performance of the measures in categorizing languages as either fixed or flexible in terms of word order. The outcomes suggest that a single, unified score for morphological intricacy may not be feasible, yet our analysis of the causes of discrepancies among the measures helps to clarify the underlying mechanisms driving the variation in language scores.

Most auction platforms provide bidders with limited information, such as bidder counts and bid price, but not crucial data like a bidder's device type or network status. This paper proposes a novel solution, Meta-Bid, to address this problem. By collaborating with auction providers and leveraging meta-information, Meta-Bid enables accurate predictions of object states. Furthermore, to showcase Meta-Bid's benefits, the authors integrate the solution with current bidding systems and conduct a comprehensive performance comparison with a leading bidding engine. The outcome shows that Meta-Bid enhances the accuracy of object state prediction and leads to increased revenue for a bidder.

This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating quantum correlations without negativity. Specifically, we investigate a scenario where two parties, A and B, perform measurements to generate quantum correlations in system A and system b, considering two scenarios: one where local operations and classical communication (LOCC) are used, and one where random access codes are used. Our findings reveal that the possibility of remotely generating quantum correlations without Wigner negativity reduces to zero as soon as local quantum correlations are accessible with certainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the no-deletion principle constrains the amount of quantum correlations that can be deleted locally. Our results also consider the case of quantum correlations without Wigner negativity and examine the relationship between these two nonclassical properties, ultimately concluding that the absence of one does not necessitate the absence of the other.

We develop an alternative, performance-based definition of security and demonstrate that the optimal secure data rate is directly proportional to the key generation rate. This definition is consistent with the performance-based definition of reliability in classical communication theory. We find that the practical QKD data rate is heavily dependent on the specific implementation. For example, when using the BB84 scheme with efficient feedback, our analysis shows that the data rate can be as high as 70 Mbit/s within 10 cm of Beijing's average daylight distance. This significant increase in data rate is achieved by optimizing the single-photon emission rate within a 20-80% range. In contrast, the traditional approach yields a data rate of only 26 Mbit/s for this same setting. Furthermore, our definition enables the analysis of secure data rates for learning attacks, where the attacker adapts to maximize the data rate of the legitimate users.

Our investigation centers on the noncommutativity effect and its role in distributing nucleon momentum among quarks and gluons. It's evident that a finite energy cutoff is necessary to prevent divergence in the noncommutative parameter limit. The cutoff implementation reveals that the momentum distribution among constituents varies significantly based on the noncommutativity level. We introduce an advanced topological model that exhibits a unique phase shift in response to localized input, such as a wave source in a one-dimensional system. This system features two topological components: a wave-generating entity that generates circular motion and a static entity that exerts an attractive force between them. As the system's size changes, the relative positions of the entities change, resulting in a localized phase shift marked by the entities being out of alignment. We found this system to be topologically protected in systems without attractive forces but get compromised by attractive forces. Nevertheless, we propose an enhanced system that remains topologically protected and produces a large phase shift at the location of the attractive force through fine-tuning. This system can be realized by combining two particles with opposite momentum with a soliton.

However, models designed for general pre-training often contain unwanted characteristics that are inherited from texts passed through a tokeniser, hindering their ability to effectively process dialogue data. To overcome this limitation, a novel language model called m2m-Dialog is developed by fine-tuning the Transformer for the task of dialogue translation without tokenisation, thereby eliminating the reliance on standard tokenisers. As a result, this model offers enhanced flexibility in the form of choice, allowing for the use of any form of data augmentation when generating responses, and can operate without requiring tokenisation during inference, a capability that proves particularly beneficial for handling unknown words or novel entities encountered during conversations. To demonstrate its capabilities in a more practical setting, m2m-Dialog is combined with GPT2 and shown to produce more coherent and context-specific responses when conditioned on a set of conversation history samples sourced from the Blended Skills Takewaway dataset.

We analyzed 45 early generation stars in NGC 2808 and 47 Tuc to explore their elemental composition, which helps to understand their star-formation process. We used the APOGEE spectra from SDSS-IV to determine metal-to-hydrogen ratios and alpha-element-to-hydrogen ratios. We applied the MOPOGEE method to find carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances. We calculated the oxygen-to-metal ratios, which matched the average in the galactic disk. We used the abundances to calculate nitrogen-to-argon and carbon-to-argon ratios, which were compared to values in the solar neighborhood. We developed a new model to describe the galactic star-formation process and used it to fit the distribution of nitrogen and carbon abundances. We analyzed the galactic star formation from 12 billion years ago to 11 billion years ago, which matched the period of the galactic disk formation. We used the same model to fit the distribution of nitrogen and carbon in 45 Tuc, which revealed that the stars formed within 1 billion years through gas with a metallicity similar to the solar value. We compared the galactic star formation in the inner regions to the regions similar to the solar neighborhood, which revealed that the galactic disk formed quickly but the regions similar to the solar neighborhood took longer to form.

Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to FG-NET, which involves annotating and training on entity types, results in two significant issues. Firstly, the entity type list is often arbitrary, and there is no single 'optimal' configuration, which means different types can be considered better or worse. Secondly, the supervised training process is time-consuming and extremely costly, especially when the type list is extensive, which makes progress slow and the process impractical for large datasets. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new framework known as FG-NEType, which allows for the automatic discovery of entity types from unclassified text. The framework consists of multiple stages, where the type list is refined and re-trained on unlabelled data using unique representations. The results from our experiments, which were based on the 2019 FG-NET dataset, show that the FG-NEType approach, which is fully unsupervised, achieved 71.02 F1, which means it outperformed the previous best results by 2.33 F1.

However, this requires accurate and continuous VM workload forecasting. Machine learning algorithms can provide load forecasts, and these, in turn, enable Proactive Load Balancing Service (PLBS) to optimize cloud resource allocation. The combination of ML algorithms and PLBS, however, poses a challenge as it involves continuously updating the VM placement every few seconds to account for changing load patterns. Since some VMS, like those using KVM, allow for fine-grained control over Linux containers, and these control mechanisms are transparent to guest virtual machines, we can utilize the affine group scheduling feature to schedule ML models without guest interference. Our load balancing approach has been validated through simulation, and results show that it can reduce average VM load by 22% and energy consumption by 14% compared to a reactive load balancing strategy.

assuming each agent acts to maximize its own objectives leads to stable equilibrium scenarios where no single agent can improve outcomes without cooperation. However, current optimization techniques focused on equilibrium solutions fall short when dealing with complex objectives that cannot be easily broken down into simpler parts. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to approximating equilibrium solutions using neural networks, particularly in cooperative games where networks can model complex objectives. However, training these approximation models is a significant challenge, especially in non-cooperative games, due to the lack of a clear learning goal. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed methods for training models that aim to optimize joint outcomes, such as Lagrangian relaxation, but these methods can only be used in specific types of games. To provide a universal learning method, we have developed a novel approach called adversarial collaborative training (ACT), which involves training a model to optimize outcomes in a game by using an adversary that simulates the actions of other agents, leading to more effective results in complex non-cooperative games compared to traditional optimization techniques.

This reorganization enables the application of innovative deep learning techniques in probabilistic collision avoidance. This paper presents a new collision avoidance approach, which builds on the Adaptive Collision Avoidance framework by utilizing VAEs to create an organized latent structure for obstacle odometry. Our proposed approach determines the odometry of an obstacle through the application of VAEs. This enables the representation of an obstacle's trajectory in the latent space, allowing for the development of a simple rule-based system that identifies the origin and progression point of an obstacle's trajectory. This information is then used to calculate the time it will take for the obstacle to pass, allowing for early avoidance actions. Our proposed approach was successfully tested in simulated scenarios, where it demonstrated comparable performance to ACAPoint, while also exhibiting comparable results in success rate and average time to pass metrics.

(A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies are now actively using experiments to inform product development, fueled by the desire to offer better user experiences. As a result, the product development process at these companies is now heavily influenced by experimentation data, leading to a shift towards a data-driven product development workflow. Despite this shift, there is a notable limitation in relying solely on experimental evidence due to the limited number of running experiments and the need for a high-fidelity estimation of treatment effect accuracy. This high-fidelity estimation is critical in making informed decisions, but it is often absent in decision-making processes at these companies. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework that provides a way to accurately estimate treatment effect accuracy in a Bayesian model, which can be used to update parameters when an experiment is conducted. By applying this framework, the product development team can update parameters in real-time as experiments are run, which enables a more accurate estimation of treatment effect accuracy. By integrating this framework into decision-making processes, the product development team can make more informed decisions by considering both experimental evidence and the accuracy of that evidence. Our case study demonstrates the benefits of this framework, which in turn improves the quality of decision-making and the flow of product development processes at a large data-driven company.

Deep Space transport is presented. The study centers on an imaginary mission to Mars and involves converting low-enriched uranium into energy using a combination of fast reactors and solid core breeder reactors. The initial conversion process involves a nuclear electric propulsion system consisting of a small reactor, a salt fueled fast reactor, a conversion unit, a magnetohydrodynamic generator, and a power turbine driving an ion thruster. The reactor's fast breeder utilizes low-enriched uranium fuel and employs a salt as a breeder and coolant in a vacuum environment. The study shows that two such reactors, operating in tandem, can generate enough energy to support the mission and includes a detailed calculation of the reactor's thermal conversion efficiency. The analysis reveals that the reactor's fuel lifetime is approximately 6 years, during which it produces 190,000 kilowatts-hour of energy. The thermal conversion efficiency is estimated at 9.2%, or 172 watts, for every kilogram of salt used. The study further demonstrates that the reactor's efficiency is optimized when the mass ratio of breeder to fast breeder is approximately 1.37.

The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A key aspect of this structure lies in the utilization of constant-size random codes generated by independent random functions. It's demonstrated that codes meeting specific divergence criteria can be efficiently identified through analysis of the structure's boundary measurements. Importantly, the probability of code failure can be precisely quantified as the size of the structure's boundary divided by the code's length is exponentially outpaced by the inverse of the logarithm of the code's size. Moreover, the probability of successful decoding can also be accurately determined as the size of the structure's boundary divided by the code's length, provided that the density of the code exceeds a critical threshold proportional to the inverse of the square root of the logarithm of the code's size. These results facilitate linear time decoding of the quantum LDPC codes through classical LDPC decoding methods.

waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the brightening of a forensic site. These shocks can either be turbulent in the absence of stable patterns or magnetic in nature, influenced by underlying magnetic fields. Although magnetic shocks have been extensively studied, the mechanisms behind turbulent shocks remain poorly understood. Specifically, researchers are seeking to understand the characteristics of turbulent shocks that give rise to type III radio bursts, a phenomenon still in the realm of theoretical inquiry. In the case studied here, a forensic site was observed to brighten in response to a solar flare on May 15, 2013, here referred to as the forensic burst. Analysis revealed that the forensic burst exhibited characteristics typical of turbulent shocks hereinafter referred to as FTSHs, including a rapid increase in brightness and frequency of electromagnetic radiation emitted as the shock accelerates electrons. These findings indicate that FTSHs differ from the magnetic shocks previously studied, instead displaying characteristics unique to turbulent shocks such as increased frequency and intensity of electromagnetic radiation in tandem with the velocity and magnitude of the shock. These distinct characteristics suggest that FTSHs may serve as an optimal means for studying electron acceleration patterns.

-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The proposed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic element, where the positions of random vortices are continually updated at a rate proportional to the local velocity, influenced by a positive definite function and a Martingale noise driven by a Brownian motion. Key findings indicate that the probability distribution of the random vortex system follows a modified version of the second Burgers equation with a stochastic component, where the amplitude of the wave is proportionally related to the standard deviation of the noise. Consequently, the resulting flow can be expressed as the sum of two separate, distinct flows - one being smooth and the other containing turbulent, dissipation-driven waves. The proposed model has practical implications in the development of reduced-order models for fluid dynamics.

the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at two distinct wavelengths. The resulting dataset covered an area of approximately 120 square degrees in the far-ultraviolet spectrum, allowing researchers to identify and eliminate artificial sources generated by the GALEX satellite's own reflectors. The remaining point sources were then analyzed, and their magnitudes in different directions were measured, revealing a symmetrical pattern with no notable variations. This continuity was observed across the complex's central plane and beyond 20 degrees in both the east and west directions. The measured flux levels were found to be consistent with those predicted by the Hadronic Cosmic Ray Machine Interactions model, indicating that the UV radiation from the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex's young stars does not significantly contribute to the observed background. Furthermore, the analysis revealed a diffuse flux of approximately 10^5 erg s^-1 sr^-1 in the far-ultraviolet spectrum, which was then used to estimate the intensity of the EUV radiation. The calculated EUV intensity was found to be around 2.5 x 10^-3 erg s^-1 cm^-2 s^-1, which was then compared to the intensity of the cosmic ray flux. The comparison showed that the EUV radiation provides enough energy to activate the cosmic ray reactions while their intensity is still high enough to explain the observed diffuse background brightness.

In the absence of specific information about the population, researchers often turn to random sampling. Utilizing spatial data however offers an alternative: Zipf's Law enables the prediction of a population size from the frequency of occurrence of a particular size class within a geographic area. This study investigates whether, when size classes are defined by intervals of $\log$ values, the empirical distribution of population sizes adheres to a smooth probability density function derived from the product of discrete, evenly-spaced $\log$-normal probability density functions. An approximation of this smooth density is considered, comprising the sum of the true densities with the exclusion of the central term. A study involving the estimation of the city population sizes serves as a test case. Results indicate a strong correlation between the estimated and true population sizes. This finding enables the development of a straightforward, effective method for the estimation of city population sizes, based on the assumption that each city occupies a unique size class. A global comparison of the biases of the estimated and the log-normal distributions through the use of the $p$-norm shows the log-normal distribution to be significantly more accurate. This study also examines the sources of bias in the estimation method. Furthermore, the study compares the performance of the log-normal distribution with that of the Zipf's Law discrete distribution model.

Despite the growing use of computer-assisted methods in qualitative research, the field of DA remains understudied. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the atom-molecule T-matrix exhibits time independence even when the molecule-atom coupling is non-zero. In this context, we discussed how dark states can be used to convert atoms into molecules and vice versa, and explored the quantum dynamics of weak molecule-atom coupling under these conditions. Specifically, we found that a stationary entanglement of atom-molecule pairs persists even with non-zero coupling, and that a scale-invariant entanglement of atom-molecule circuits is formed over time. Furthermore, we discussed other aspects of this system, including its similarity to models of fermion pairing and photon optics in optical cavities, and the existence of pair solitons in certain parameter regimes. In particular, we found that pair solitons can be used to efficiently convert atoms into molecules and vice versa, and demonstrated their stability in certain parameter regimes. In addition, we discussed other mechanisms for coherent atom-molecule conversion that may be realizable in experiments, including those involving optical lattices and optical cavities.

"Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the primary groups, with the latter aiming to dominate the former through strategic murder missions. In the event of a mafia victory, the number of murders committed by the mafia typically equals the number of mafia members. This study presents a mathematical model, representing the game as a tree, to analyze the likelihood of a mafia win. Our model encompasses various game characteristics, including random and targeted killings, the ability to see dead victims, and the ability to discuss strategy. To develop an accurate representation of the game as a tree, we must account for the complexity introduced by simultaneous events and the nearly infinite number of possible game states. To address this challenge, we represent the game as a tree with nodes representing six distinct conditions, with each condition representing a unique set of game characteristics, such as the number of kills and the number of mafia members. This approach enables us to capture the complexity of the game and its various outcomes. In the event of a mafia win, the number of kills by the mafia is modeled as a binomial distribution, with parameters equal to the number of mafia members and the fraction of the population representing the mafia. This representation allows us to calculate the likelihood of a particular number of kills by the mafia.

Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite the increasing complexity and size of modern models. This paper presents a novel algorithm called NeuMoE, a derivative-free, model-parallel method for learning MoE models. In contrast to existing baselines, NeuMoE is capable of escaping local optima and consistently yields reliable results, independent of model scale or architecture choice. At its core, NeuMoE employs a dynamic gating mechanism to determine the gradient direction and magnitude for each expert, based on its conditionality likelihood. In extensive experiments, NeuMoE consistently outperformed baseline methods across various settings and benchmark datasets, achieving superior performance with significantly fewer iterations and a much larger model. Notably, NeuMoE successfully learned large, complex models with expert counts ranging from 256 to 4096, a feat previously unachievable with existing baselines.

Two of these sources, located near the base of the cluster's double star population's rotation axis, exhibit characteristics of red giant branch (RGB) X-ray sources. Their FUV to X-ray flux ratios are found to be significantly higher than those observed in the field. The third source, positioned at the center of NGC 4147, shows a variable X-ray flux with a longer timescale than typically observed in RGB X-ray sources. We determined the energy spectra of all four sources and found them to be consistent with those of isolated RGB X-ray sources. Their luminosities range from 10$^{30}$ to 10$^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$. We discuss the characteristics of the identified sources and one additional source at the cluster's edge, which may also be an RGB X-ray source.

A key challenge in DTL is a little understood phenomenon called knowledge degradation, which occurs when features are transferred from one task to another.  Currently, the best way to address this issue is through selective transfer learning (STL), which involves selecting relevant training data to build new models.  Despite its potential benefits, STL relies on human oversight and is therefore prone to errors.  To address these limitations, we introduce a new, promising approach called top-down query (TDQ).  In contrast to conventional methods, TDQ asks machines to identify new features from the differences between tasks.  Our experiments with this novel approach have yielded impressive results across various tasks and datasets, including a 54% improvement over existing transfer learning methods.  Furthermore, TDQ has been shown to work effectively even when features are transferred between tasks with significant differences.  Our research also reveals that TDQ is a reliable and robust solution to the problem of knowledge degradation in deep transfer learning.

Our theoretical model, based on the composite fermion Landau levels, demonstrates that this phase shift is a natural consequence of the chiral symmetry. One challenge with text classification is dealing with imbalanced data, which often occurs when one class dominates the others. This difficulty is common across various NLP tasks and datasets. Another related issue is dataset shift, which occurs when the distribution of labeled data differs from the unseen test data. State-of-the-art text classification models often perform poorly under these conditions. To address this, researchers developed a technique called TS-Timespace, which is an over-sampling method for text classification. This method involves generating more instances of the minority class in imbalanced data by introducing minor modifications to the samples, which are then combined with the original data to form a new dataset. To prevent the artificially enhanced data from affecting model performance, TS-Timespace involves training two different neural network models on the original and artificially enhanced data, which are then integrated for accurate prediction on the test data. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-Timespace outperforms other state-of-the-art algorithms in text classification.

However, previous research showed that the basic and adaptive ANS encoders take a considerable amount of time to complete the encoding process when a large amount of data is provided. This paper proposes two solutions to address this issue by limiting the frequency of table updates during the ANS encoding process, resulting in better compression performance compared to existing methods. The proposed techniques, called frequency-constrained and tree-structured ANS, yield an average compression ratio of 4.01 bits per symbol, which is very close to the standard ANS's 4.01 bits per symbol. oporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and presence of liquid phases. Our study delves into how the dielectric behavior of these materials evolves as a function of composition and liquid content. We employed molecular dynamics simulations using the RISM-MIL models to analyze aqueous mixtures of silicates and silica, allowing us to calculate structural and dielectric properties for various systems. By examining different compositions, we investigated how the dielectric behavior responds to changes in concentration and phase. Our research revealed that incorporating water into silica causes a significant decrease in dielectric constant, whereas mixtures of silicate and water exhibit two distinct regimes: a low-concentration phase with reduced dielectric constant and a high-concentration phase with increased dielectric constant, similar to that of aqueous systems. These findings demonstrate that the dielectric behavior of these materials can be understood through the relationship between composition, structure, and dielectric properties.

Drones used in UK airspace have evolved over two decades, starting with the first approved flight in 1998. These drones hold various applications including aerial mapping, surveillance, broadcast events, military operations, and educational settings. Over time, drones have been used in several high-profile incidents including delivering life-saving blood to Welsh patients and capturing court evidence in rape trials. As drones continue to progress, both technological advancements and increased public acceptance drive the progression of drone development. Onwards from 2019, the UK Air Navigation Order 2016 grants drone operators freedom of flight, freeing them from previous restrictions. These changes create an opportunity to re-examine drones within the context of collective intelligence and swarm behavior. This paper presents an innovative approach to drones as an intelligent swarm, taking into consideration their growing presence and potential in modern society.

We investigate the topology of a non-Hermitian system when correlation is involved, focusing on an extended non-Hermitian Chern insulator with broken parity-time symmetry. Within the non-Hermitian bulk phase, the system's correlation causes a transition from the Hermitian to the non-Hermitian Kondo disorder fixed point as the interaction strength increases. Our findings reveal that this correlation-driven transition triggers a non-Hermitian skin mode that emerges from the Hermitian to the non-Hermitian fixed point. The skin mode is characterized by exceptional points at the Fermi level, marking a turning point between the Hermitian and non-Hermitian bulk phases. Furthermore, the correlation-induced transition facilitates a non-Hermitian Anderson localization phase that arises from the non-Hermitian bulk phase. The correlation due to electron-electron interactions shifts the Anderson localization phase boundary, moving it to a weaker hopping strength requirement compared to the non-interacting model. The understanding gained from this study sheds light on the role of electron correlation in non-Hermitian systems, paving the way for future research in this field to be simplified.

mechanics has been developed, referred to as epistemic superdeterminism. This theory attributes the seemingly random nature of quantum events to the ignorance of the system's internal observer, resulting in predictions that match those of quantum mechanics. Due to its superdeterministic nature, this theory appears resistant to the challenge posed by Bell's theorem, which asserts that local hidden variables cannot replicate the predictions of quantum mechanics. However, it is demonstrated that the epistemic superdeterministic theory falls short in explaining certain critical aspects of real-world experiments, specifically the consistency of random numbers generated by vacuum detection and the distinct differences observed in Bell-type experiments. These discrepancies provide concrete evidence that refutes the notion that the world can be explained by the internal perspective of the system's observer, suggesting that the theory of quantum mechanics remains fundamentally probabilistic in nature.

by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times,  $\tau_y$ and  $\tau_z$, corresponding to particles approaching a potential barrier in the $y$ or $z$ direction. There is a discrepancy between the standard definition of tunneling time and the Larmor clock measurement. The latter two clocks, Larmor and Lichten, show a relationship through the Larmor frequency. Notably, the Lichten clock measures a time that is half of  $\tau_y$ or  $\tau_z$. To resolve this discrepancy with the standard tunneling time, a new model is developed based on Larmor clock measurements. This model utilizes a superposition of particles approaching the barrier in both the Larmor clock's coordinate system and normal coordinate system to derive an expression for  $\tau_y$. The new expression reveals that  $\tau_y$ is the average of Larmor and Lichten clock times. Further investigation shows that both  $\tau_y$ and  $\tau_z$ are influenced by quantum interference, occurring before the particles enter the barrier. Consequently, both tunneling times are expected to decrease as the barrier approaches, contradicting Lichten's prediction that quantum interference has no effect on his clock measurement.

By utilizing our new approach, we demonstrate that solutions to these games can be accurately described in terms of a reduced-order model, where the state process is condensed into a low-dimensional representation. Under specific conditions, we establish the existence and continuity of these reduced-order solutions, while providing error bounds that validate their precision. Furthermore, we show that our approach allows for the efficient computation of these solutions through a two-step process involving an initial reduction of the original game into an equivalent finite-horizon formulation, followed by the extraction of a low-dimensional model from this new formulation. We illustrate the effectiveness of our theoretical results with a concrete example of a financial game, where one player seeks to manipulate the price of a credit derivative, while the issuer responds by adopting the optimal strategy from an infinite array of possibilities.

Integral-Derivative (PID) control approach integrated with Sliding Mode Dynamic Vorabic Control (SMDVC) for stabilizing oscillations in a space satellite. The model of the satellite, based on Euler-Lagrange equations with constraints, exhibits non-linear characteristics throughout its motion. To address non-linearity, this work employs the Smooth Chebyshev Function (SCF) method for modeling and analyzing non-linear functions. Following this, a smooth note function is determined, and Taylor series are calculated to establish a smooth mathematical model for control purposes. Using the Lagrange principle, the SCF method is further developed to determine the torque of the control, and a sliding mode variable structure control is introduced to estimate parameters for attitude control. To verify the efficacy of the proposed SMDVC-PID, simulations are conducted, demonstrating the algorithm's ability to maintain a consistent frequency and achieve desired amplitude while estimating parameters through sliding mode for a wide range of simulations.

This dataset includes event observations from multiple space-based solar observatories and global solar image data, enabling a comprehensive understanding of solar activity. Our focus is on analyzing the temporal and spatial behavior of local events and their correlation with typical solar activity patterns, such as the solar cycle. We have also created a machine learning model to forecast the local energy releases based on historical data from the Sun's polar regions and equatorial activity. Our research indicates that there is a notable 11-year cycle in local event counts, with statistical connections observed between events and other solar activity patterns, including coronal mass ejections and flares. Our forecasting model shows promise, with certain configurations predicting up to a 2-week advance warning of energetic proton events detected by ground-based observatories.

to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it puts a limit on how much gluon can be added to a parton with a given fraction $x$.  As a result, high-energy processes continue with a plateau in gluon density at low values of $x$, independent of energy.  In contrast to this saturation trend, at high energies above the transition scale and at high $x$ values greater than a certain threshold, $p_T$-distribution of charged particles continues with a growing dependence on energy.  By combining data on high-energy heavy-ion collisions and $x$-dependence of parton distributions from the parton saturation model, we can obtain an integrated knowledge on $x$-dependence of parton density at different values of $x$ and energy.  By applying this understanding, we can predict the energy dependence of subleading flow coefficients in high-energy heavy-ion collisions.

Due to the presence of a U(1) gauge symmetry, two types of collective excitations emerge: long-waved, Drude-like transport modes and short-waved, confined magnons. The background dependence of the CMs is so strong that their linear damping limits differ qualitatively, with the high-waved part behaving like a lower-energy density mode, while the low-waved part retains its higher energy density characteristics. This background dependence of the CMs is expected to be observable in both the optical absorption and KEEM experiments.

When errors do occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this phenomenon is the creation of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point sources in typical scanning patterns. A recent study found that to accurately estimate CMB maps, these instrumental effects must be removed, a task that can be achieved through a non-Gaussian de-correlation process. Although previously proposed methods for removing instrumental effects after maximum likelihood processing exist, these can introduce statistical noise into maps with strong source signals, leading to a decrease in signal-to-noise ratios. For more sensitive measurements of faint sources and accurate CMB map estimation, more robust removal of instrumental effects is required. We have established a set of tools that first removes the sinusoidal patterns induced by source structures due to non-Gaussian de-correlation, then applies an algorithm to remove residual effects. This method has been tested using simulated data and verified using 100 GHz StudeSF data.

Like state tomography, the process tomography involves a multitude of measurements, but researchers have found ways to lower the required number of measurements. Specifically, recent discoveries allow for a minimal number of measurements to characterize a quantum process using its spectral data, mirroring the approach developed for state tomography. Building upon the convex form of the process fidelity, the process's spectral data can be derived from as few as M (M+1)/2 measurements, where M represents the highest eigenvalue of the process's matrix. Notably, the process's spectral data can be obtained from fewer measurements than the process's matrix elements when M exceeds two. Moreover, the proposed method allows for estimating the process's spectral elements with an optimal lower lower bound of (3/M) probability, achieved by maximizing the process's spectral element with a given measurement outcome, a finding confirmed by the process's eigenvalue decomposition. The method's effectiveness was demonstrated using random quantum processes and confirmed using Amplitudes quantum hardware.

It quantifies phase with high precision in its ideal form, yet phase inaccuracies are introduced when noise is present. Ramassey sequences have been extensively employed in nuclear magnetic resonance for precise phase measurement, though only a limited number have been used to simulate the effects of noise. This research presents a comprehensive set of Ramsey sequences that enables the accurate simulation of various noise phenomena affecting a two-level system, including the scattering of electromagnetic waves and interactions with environmental heat sources. , Klein, and Le stated an unresolved problem regarding the minimum depth of a rooted complete $k$-ary tree's balanced binary subtree. We've found the solution: any binary subtree of a complete $k$-ary tree with $n$ nodes has depth at most $\log_{k}3n$. We've achieved this by counting the binary subtree's nodes via a $k$-ary number representation, applying the binary subtree's pruning principle, and using the properties of balanced equations. Additionally, our method extends to binary trees by solving the minimum depth; the solution derives from a theorem illustrating the relationship between the binary subtree's nodes and the number of non-zero digits in its $k$-ary representation. We've also developed an algorithm based on binary search to compute this depth.

with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. In this study, we investigate the dynamic pattern of variational ansatz construction (VAC) error propagation, focusing on the effect of ansatz size and error distribution on the accumulation of error across the ansatz. We then develop two techniques, circuit rotation adjustment (CRA) and singular value decomposition (SVD), to control error propagation by determining optimal circuit parameter values and selecting relevant ansatz components. We demonstrate that these methods effectively mitigate error propagation, enabling the accurate solution of smaller systems and the reliable construction of deep ansatz for use in more complex applications. Our findings have significant implications for the development of NISQ-era quantum algorithms and the scaling up of VQA algorithms to utilize deeper ansatze with lesser precision.

Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we introduce a novel approach, Aspect-based sentiment analysis using neural networks and eye-tracking data. Our method begins by utilizing BERT to generate context and aspect embeddings that capture the aspect's influence on the context. Next, we integrate these embeddings into a Long Short-Term Memory network to simulate human-aware sentiment comprehension. Additionally, we incorporate eye-tracking data to enrich the understanding of implicit sentiment, then leverage a self-attention mechanism to combine these embeddings. Our proposed model also employs a binary classifier to distinguish between sentiment labels and neutral aspects, allowing us to frame the problem as a binary classification task. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on implicit sentiment across multiple datasets.

case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our calculation of logistic regression parameters relies on weighted estimates from the secondary outcome, where weights consider both the stratification and selection indicators. By leveraging weighted regression techniques, we develop a procedure for mediation analysis. Specifically, we identify sufficient conditions under which the estimated mediation effect is unbiased when using the weighted least squares estimator. Our approach allows for the estimation of the direct effect in stratified case-control studies, where the stratification variables are correlated with the primary outcome. Our methodology is validated through simulations and applied to an actual study investigating the link between statin use, low-density lipoprotein levels, and cardiovascular events.

nonlinear optical systems has become the standard technology for developing high-power lasers, typically based on chirp-compressed seed lasers. However, directly amplifying narrowband laser pulses leads to severe compressor problems due to their natural frequency chirp, which poses a major challenge. We propose an innovative approach, which utilizes digital holographic phase retrieval to counteract frequency chirp and enables direct amplification of unchirped frequency-comb laser seeds. By merging advanced phase retrieval techniques and Fourier-domain compression, this method eliminates the need for external compression and enhances the stability of the amplification process. Moreover, its high sensitivity allows for the detection of minute frequency changes, which makes it an effective tool for diagnosing and controlling complex NLO systems.

Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity adjustment technique for the Large Hadron Collider. These scans involved rapidly varying the beta-star value of the collision point to obtain the transverse beam emittance within a few minutes. we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing three locations' labels allows us to deduce the shortest path between any two of the points. Our work focuses on the fault-tolerant version of this problem in weighted graphs with no cycles. We've established that determining whether a graph requires at least $k$ labels for this labelling is NP-hard, requiring at least $O(n^d)$ time. Building on this, we've found that the problem remains NP-hard in trees, $K_2$-free planar graphs, meshed planar graphs, and simple tournaments when restricted to these specific graph types. To tackle this problem, we've developed an efficient labelling method for trees that uses up to $O(k\log (kn))$ labels and works for any $k$ size description. Extendible from trees to $K_2$-free planar graphs, this method maintains the same label bound while addressing the fault-tolerant labelling problem. However, we've found these labelings aren't necessarily optimal as we've created an instance requiring $k+1$ labels when our method would use $k$. Additionally, we've found an efficient labelling for meshed planar graphs but we've created an instance demonstrating that the labelings aren't necessarily optimal in these cases either.

to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicks. One such device is the shot noise timer, which utilizes the intermittent electrical current from a photon source to keep time. Although the time intervals between clicks are unpredictable, averaging over a large number of events yields a consistent output, making it a viable method of time measurement. Notably, even with perfect electronic processing, the accuracy of these devices is restricted by the shot noise limit. We will explore an alternative approach, using a source of resonant photons with a long-lasting lifespan, such as atomic ensembles or solid-state systems with long-lived qubits, to create an accurate timekeeping device. By utilizing phase-shift keying, we can design a timer that can achieve precision well beyond the shot noise limit, paving the way for the development of highly reliable and accurate random timekeeping devices.

The dynamic nature of energy harvesting SWDNs makes traditional traffic engineering challenges even more complex. To overcome these difficulties, the problem is reformulated as a mathematical optimization problem with the aim of maximizing network utility while ensuring energy constraints. Since solving the problem using an optimal algorithm is computationally impractical due to its NP-hard property, a distributed control plane with two proposed algorithms is utilized as an alternative solution. The algorithms learn optimal solutions through iterative updates in a decentralized manner, with the first algorithm converging to a optimal solution at the cost of high computational complexity. To address this issue, the second algorithm is introduced as a low-complexity alternative with guaranteed convergence to a sub-optimal solution.

While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays is more reflective of real-world applications, but raises additional technical obstacles. In the experts scenario with complete knowledge, we create an algorithm achieving a first-order regret bound, highlighting the relationship between delays and losses. This algorithm also results in a first-order regret bound for bandits, given knowledge of when arms are available. However, these bounds are worsened by a factor of time and arm size, respectively, in comparison to standard regret bounds. When arm-dependent delays are randomly distributed, we provide a simpler bound for any algorithm in both the experts and bandits settings. Notably, our algorithm ensures regret does not grow with the size of arm-dependent delays in the experts scenario. This work is foundational, as direct applications to online learning problems are scarce. Yet, considering a payment scheme in the experts scenario, delay-dependent losses are equivalent to being paid per request. In the bandits scenario, our result can be applied to best-arm identification, leading to a time-complexity bound worsened by arm-dependent factors. However, this is typical in arm-dependent settings. We also analyze an application to a payment problem where losses are paid per request. In the best-arm identification problem, our result is known to be tight.

-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has far-reaching consequences, surpassing the impact of SARS and H1N1/09 viruses. The rapid dissemination can be attributed to the widespread use of the internet and air travel. The scientific community's initial response relies on applying established concepts to a newly emerging pathogen. The US National Strategic Plan outlines a multi-phased approach for managing an infectious disease outbreak, involving detection, mitigation, containment, and recovery phases. The detection of an infectious disease typically relies on surveillance systems, such as the US Influenza-like illness surveillance system. A COVID-19 thermal scanner was developed to enhance detection efficiency and reduce reliance on contact tracing methods. The scanner's initial prototype was tested in a real-world setting to validate its effectiveness. The scanner's design features a unique ventilation system to minimize testing area constraints, allowing for the evaluation of multiple individuals within a reasonable time frame. The scanner's performance was assessed using a large dataset of unannotated images, demonstrating its potential for accurate and efficient disease detection.

Recent advancements in neuroscience and quantum physics have led to theories that attempt to explain the nature of consciousness, ranging from new neurological models and pharmacological studies to speculative theories such as Integrated Information Theory and Quantum Consciousness. These theories have sparked intense discussion and criticism, with some arguing that they offer significant insights into the nature of consciousness, while others contend that they lack scientific credibility. In this context, we argue that the shared characteristic of these theories is their attempt to provide an explanatory framework for the complexities of consciousness, rather than their individual merits. By viewing these theories through the lens of philosophical epistemology, we argue that the cumulative effect of research in this field, rather than individual achievements, holds the key to understanding its progress. In particular, we examine how research in this field can be evaluated using the principles of Bayesian evidence and the distinction between top-down and bottom-up scientific inquiry. By analyzing the research in this field through these lenses, we conclude that the central nervous system remains an incompletely understood phenomenon, with the research in this field as a whole indicating that the nature of consciousness remains poorly understood.

Monocular 3D object pose estimation involves creating a 3D representation of an object from a 2D image alone, which is a complex task. Most current methods employ a two-step process, first localizing the object in 2D and then calculating its 3D pose. However, objects in real-world images often appear distorted due to occlusions, clutter, and camera distortions, making it a challenging task. Most current datasets and methods also rely on easily manipulable objects, such as cubes and blocks, which does not accurately represent the complex real-world scenarios encountered in applications such as robotic grasping and self-driving vehicles. This paper proposes a new, single-stage method called MeshPose, which utilizes a different representation of 3D objects, specifically mesh coordinates, to improve 6-DoF pose estimation. By directly predicting the 3D transformation matrix from the 3D mesh, this method outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage methods, which are often brittle and prone to overfitting. Additionally, this work aims to bridge the gap between current datasets and real-world scenarios by focusing on estimating the pose of randomly placed objects, which is a more realistic task.

The study found no correlation between the speed of sound and the temperature near sunspots, which suggests that the speed of sound may be affected by the presence of magnetic fields. Our approach focuses on four key aspects: population, urban infrastructure, municipal services, and urban economy, using visualizations and statistics to provide a holistic overview of urban conditions. By making these reports publicly available for free, we aim to facilitate data-driven decision making and foster a culture of data sharing and awareness.

Every conformal field theory can be integrated into a Toda conformal field theory. Toda conformal field theory's current algebras are formed through the deformation of Virasoro algebras. Toda conformal field theory's operators are formed through the deformation of Virasoro algebras' modes. Toda conformal field theory's current algebras' deformations also incorporate the deformation of bosonic galleries and Galilean algebras. Toda conformal field theory's background fields are related to the commutative background fields of the underlying free field theory. Traditional studies on the Strauss process involved analysis under a fixed distance parameter 'r'. However, research can now be conducted by varying this parameter, allowing for both large and small values where the process exhibits distinct properties. This paper explores the properties of the Strauss process when its parameter 'r' is very large or very small. When 'r' is very large, the process converges to a Poisson point process on a two-dimensional plane, demonstrating independence from clustering or anti-clustering behavior. On the other hand, when 'r' is very small, the process becomes a Poisson point process on a two-dimensional plane with a circular area of radius 'r', excluding any form of spatial clustering or anti-clustering behavior outside this circular area. This paper also establishes mathematical theorems and proofs for these properties and their implications in determining the mean and variance of the Strauss process. These results are particularly useful in non-homogeneous Strauss process density cases where the mean and variance of the process are difficult to directly calculate, and they can be approximated by considering circular approximations of the Strauss process with large and small radii.

Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies have shown that stable matchings are achieved even when preferences are partial and probabilistic. Building on these findings, our work explores the situation in which agents submit not only partial but also varied preference lists. To address this, we develop a new approach that converts any set of partial and probabilistic preferences into a perfect matching, and then extends the existing algorithms to analyze the distribution of sizes within the resulting matchings. What's more, our methods allow for an accurate estimation of the chances of smaller sizes among these matchings. Our findings demonstrate that the size distribution of sizes follows a specific pattern, which can be calculated by combining two components - the distribution of sizes within the perfect matchings achieved through the original algorithms and the chances associated with each of these matchings.

Our proposed YACD framework addresses this divide by showcasing exceptional performance in both isolated camera settings and full scene reconstruction scenarios. YACD's unique two-stage design first projects 3D detection to 2D, and then to 3D, leveraging this asymmetry for enhanced performance. YACD's volumetric design enables it to seamlessly integrate with existing 3D detection methods, where its volume is used as input to conventional 3D detectors. Our framework's overall performance is showcased on the nuScenes dataset, where it outperforms the state-of-the-art by 5.6% in isolated camera settings and 2.4% in full scene reconstruction scenarios.

By leveraging large-margin principles inspired by support vector machines, we develop a principled way to evaluate clustering stability through the determination of a suitable, distance-based transformation matrix T. Furthermore, we establish that the determined transformation matrix T has an effective upper bound $\lambda$ for any number n of points in the dataset. This achievement affords several key outcomes: 1) a clustering stability margin that can be accurately calculated; 2) a general upper limit for any dissimilarity-based clustering algorithm; and 3) theoretical validation of a previously conjectured bound.

Deferred Neural Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic images. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging. This study introduces an innovative Deep Learning architecture, VILIRNet, for analyzing combined visible-infrared imaging. The network leverages a residual learning approach to refine visible-infrared imaging, increasing the distinctiveness of subtle and hidden wildfire features. Furthermore, a cross-domain feature fusion strategy is applied to enable the model to utilize information from both visible and infrared sources. The model incorporates a cross-domain feature fusion block, consisting of two convolutional layers sharing weights, to facilitate fusing low-level features. Cross-domain feature fusion blocks can be added to the model's forward path to capture high-level features. The model's cross-domain feature fusion strategy facilitates the sharing and passing of information between visible and infrared domains, allowing the model to effectively analyze combined visible-infrared imaging. Comprehensive experiments were conducted using a custom-built dataset consisting of 1,500 fire-positive and 9,500 fire-negative images. Results indicate that VILIRNet outperforms other models, achieving an AUC of 97.38% and AUC of 95.11% on visible and infrared imaging respectively.

a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges.

itivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. This paper develops a generalized framework for conducting such an analysis, which can be applied to a wide range of statistical models. By employing a Bayesian approach, we derive a comprehensive expression for the posterior uncertainty in a model output, taking into account both random variations and variations due to various input parameters. This framework is then applied to two complex physics-based models for different astrophysical applications, namely supernovae and proto-brown dwarf models. By utilizing a Monte-Carlo based approach, we generate various realizations of these models and conduct a parameter space exploration to evaluate the model output uncertainties. We find that the most significant factors contributing to these uncertainties are typically a small subset of the total parameters. We believe that this framework, along with the novel approach to computing the model output uncertainties, will be a valuable tool for conducting such astrophysical investigations and provide a systematic method to evaluate the associated uncertainties.
